title: Safety Culture
learningObjectives: Define safety culture and distinguish it from safety climate
Describe the characteristics of a positive safety culture
Explain behavioural-based safety (BBS) and its application
Identify the role of leadership in shaping safety culture

content.text: The shared values, beliefs, attitudes, and behaviours related to safety that are ingrained in an organisation. It is 'the way we do things around here' regarding safety. Culture is deep, enduring, and driven from the top.

A snapshot of the current attitudes and perceptions of workers about safety at a given point in time. Climate is measurable via surveys and can change more quickly than culture. A positive climate reflects a positive culture.
Safety culture is the CAUSE; safety climate is the EFFECT. A positive safety culture results in a positive safety climate, which leads to better safety performance.
Characteristics of a Positive Safety Culture
Researchers from the UK Health and Safety Executive (HSE) and the International Nuclear Safety Advisory Group (INSAG) have identified the following as hallmarks of a positive safety culture:

items: Management commitment — Leaders visibly prioritise safety and allocate adequate resources
Just culture — Workers feel safe to report near misses and errors without fear of blame
Learning culture — The organisation learns from incidents and near misses
Informed culture — Those who manage and operate the system have current knowledge about human, technical, and organisational factors
Flexible culture — The ability to adapt to changing circumstances and risk levels
Communication — Open, two-way communication about safety at all levels

content.text: Behavioural-Based Safety (BBS) is an approach that focuses on identifying and changing at-risk behaviours before they lead to incidents. It is based on the observation that most incidents involve unsafe acts.

items: Step 1 — Identify critical safe and at-risk behaviours through analysis
Step 2 — Observe workers performing tasks and record behaviours
Step 3 — Provide immediate, positive feedback for safe behaviours
Step 4 — Discuss at-risk behaviours non-punitively and identify barriers
Step 5 — Analyse data to identify systemic issues
Step 6 — Set improvement targets and track progress

content.text: BBS works on positive reinforcement — reward safe behaviour rather than punish unsafe behaviour. The goal is to make safe behaviour the norm, not compliance driven by fear.

Research consistently shows that leadership is the single most important driver of safety culture. Visible leadership commitment to safety — demonstrated through actions, not just words — has a direct impact on incident rates.

rows: Most effective — inspires workers to value safety intrinsically. Leaders set vision, mentor, and lead by example.
Moderate — manages safety through rules, rewards, and consequences. Produces compliance but not commitment.
Negative — passive leadership that ignores safety issues creates a culture where risk-taking is normalised.

content.text: Saudi Aramco's management openly participates in safety walks and 'Life-Saving Rules' campaigns. ADNOC's corporate HSE culture is driven by CEO-level visible commitment. Gulf employers expect HSE professionals to promote leadership engagement in safety — this is a common interview topic.
Patrick Hudson developed a widely-used model that describes five levels of safety culture maturity:

rows: Safety is integrated into all business decisions. Proactive and continuously improving.
Safety issues are anticipated and addressed before incidents occur.
Systems-based management. Data collected but not always acted upon. 'Safety by the numbers.'
Safety is only addressed after an incident occurs. 'We fix problems as they arise.'
Safety is not a priority. 'We don't care as long as we don't get caught.'

content.text: A Gulf construction company at the 'Reactive' level has no formal HSE plan. After a fatal fall, they install guardrails on all open edges. They have moved to 'Calculative' when they then start tracking near-miss statistics. They reach 'Proactive' when they begin conducting pre-task risk assessments for every new activity before anyone starts work.
